Methods · Part II

Vectors and matrices

Units 4–6 · 17 methods

Part II (PDF) All parts

Units 4–6: vectors, matrices, and the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix. The methods build on one another. The cross product gives a plane its normal, row reduction gives both an inverse and an eigenvector, and the powers of a matrix come from its eigenvectors.

Unit 4 · Vectors

The notes · The problems

Six methods, three on the two products and three on lines and planes. The vector between two points opens Method 4.4, normalising is a step of Method 4.3, and proofs from the dot-product rules follow Method 4.1; a linear combination is found directly, by matching components, and two vectors are independent exactly when neither is a multiple of the other.

4.1 The angle between vectors, and between planes

Problem. Find the angle between two vectors in R2\mathbb{R}^2R2, R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 or Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn, where its cosine is the cosine similarity; find the angle between two planes.

Method

  1. Collect the ingredients: u⋅v\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}u⋅v, ∥u∥\left\|\mathbf{u}\right\|∥u∥ and ∥v∥\left\|\mathbf{v}\right\|∥v∥. If the vectors join points, form them first by subtracting coordinates, PQ→=(q1−p1, q2−p2, q3−p3)\overrightarrow{PQ}=(q_1-p_1,\,q_2-p_2,\,q_3-p_3)PQ​=(q1​−p1​,q2​−p2​,q3​−p3​).

  2. Divide: cos⁡θ=u⋅v∥u∥ ∥v∥\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\left\|\mathbf{u}\right\|\,\left\|\mathbf{v}\right\|}cosθ=∥u∥∥v∥u⋅v​, simplified. The sign of u⋅v\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}u⋅v alone gives the type of angle: positive acute, negative obtuse, zero a right angle.

  3. Give θ\thetaθ in [0,π][0,\pi][0,π]: exactly if cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ is a standard value, otherwise the exact cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ and then θ≈…∘\theta\approx\ldots^\circθ≈…∘.

  4. Two planes: read the normals off the coefficients. The plane ax+by+cz=dax+by+cz=dax+by+cz=d has normal (a,b,c)(a,b,c)(a,b,c).

  5. Take steps 1–3 on the normals, and report the acute angle between the planes, from ∣cos⁡θ∣\left|\cos\theta\right|∣cosθ∣.

Variants. Orthogonality is the case u⋅v=0\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=0u⋅v=0. A proof from the dot-product rules writes each squared length as a dot product, ∥w∥2=w⋅w\left\|\mathbf{w}\right\|^2=\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{w}∥w∥2=w⋅w, expands, naming each rule it uses (distributive, scalar, commutative), and simplifies to the claim.

Example Find the angle between u=(1,−2,1)\mathbf{u}=(1,-2,1)u=(1,−2,1) and v=(−2,1,1)\mathbf{v}=(-2,1,1)v=(−2,1,1), and the angle between the planes x+2y−2z=1x+2y-2z=1x+2y−2z=1 and −4x+3z=2-4x+3z=2−4x+3z=2.

The ingredients are u⋅v=−2−2+1=−3\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=-2-2+1=-3u⋅v=−2−2+1=−3, ∥u∥=1+4+1=6\left\|\mathbf{u}\right\|=\sqrt{1+4+1}=\sqrt6∥u∥=1+4+1​=6​ and ∥v∥=4+1+1=6\left\|\mathbf{v}\right\|=\sqrt{4+1+1}=\sqrt6∥v∥=4+1+1​=6​. So cos⁡θ=−36 6=−12,\cos\theta=\frac{-3}{\sqrt6\,\sqrt6}=-\frac12 ,cosθ=6​6​−3​=−21​, a standard value, and θ=2π3=120∘\boxed{\theta=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}=120^\circ}θ=32π​=120∘​: obtuse, as the negative dot product said.

The normals are n1=(1,2,−2)\mathbf{n}_1=(1,2,-2)n1​=(1,2,−2) and n2=(−4,0,3)\mathbf{n}_2=(-4,0,3)n2​=(−4,0,3), with n1⋅n2=−4+0−6=−10\mathbf{n}_1\cdot\mathbf{n}_2=-4+0-6=-10n1​⋅n2​=−4+0−6=−10, ∥n1∥=3\left\|\mathbf{n}_1\right\|=3∥n1​∥=3 and ∥n2∥=5\left\|\mathbf{n}_2\right\|=5∥n2​∥=5. So cos⁡θ=−103⋅5=−23,\cos\theta=\frac{-10}{3\cdot5}=-\frac23 ,cosθ=3⋅5−10​=−32​, not a standard value. The acute angle between the planes has ∣cos⁡θ∣=23\left|\cos\theta\right|=\tfrac23∣cosθ∣=32​: cos⁡θ=23,θ≈48.2∘\boxed{\cos\theta=\tfrac23},\qquad\allowbreak \boxed{\theta\approx48.2^\circ}cosθ=32​​,θ≈48.2∘​

Check. The law of cosines, from which the formula came: u−v=(3,−3,0)\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}=(3,-3,0)u−v=(3,−3,0) has ∥u−v∥2=18\left\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\right\|^2=18∥u−v∥2=18, and ∥u∥2+∥v∥2−2∥u∥∥v∥cos⁡θ=6+6+6=18\left\|\mathbf{u}\right\|^2+\left\|\mathbf{v}\right\|^2-2\left\|\mathbf{u}\right\|\left\|\mathbf{v}\right\|\cos\theta=6+6+6=18∥u∥2+∥v∥2−2∥u∥∥v∥cosθ=6+6+6=18. For the planes, the reversed normal (4,0,−3)(4,0,-3)(4,0,−3) describes the same second plane, as 4x−3z=−24x-3z=-24x−3z=−2, and gives cos⁡θ=1015=23\cos\theta=\tfrac{10}{15}=\tfrac23cosθ=1510​=32​ directly.

Pitfalls

  • Stopping at the dot product. u⋅v=−3\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=-3u⋅v=−3 is not the cosine, which always lies in [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1]: divide by the lengths.

  • Reporting 131.8∘131.8^\circ131.8∘ for the planes. That is the angle between the chosen normals; the planes meet at the acute angle, from ∣cos⁡θ∣\left|\cos\theta\right|∣cosθ∣.

  • Building a normal from the right-hand side. Only the coefficients of xxx, yyy and zzz make it, and a missing variable gives a 000, as in (−4,0,3)(-4,0,3)(−4,0,3).

4.2 Projection, resolving, work

Problem. Project one vector onto another; resolve a vector into a part along a direction and a part across it; find the work done by a force and its component along the motion.

Method

  1. Compute u⋅v\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}u⋅v and ∥v∥2=v⋅v\left\|\mathbf{v}\right\|^2=\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}∥v∥2=v⋅v.

  2. The projection of u\mathbf{u}u onto v\mathbf{v}v is the multiple of v\mathbf{v}v proj⁡vu=u⋅v∥v∥2 v.\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}=\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\left\|\mathbf{v}\right\|^2}\,\mathbf{v}.projv​u=∥v∥2u⋅v​v.

  3. To resolve u\mathbf{u}u: the parallel part is u∥=proj⁡vu\mathbf{u}_\parallel=\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}u∥​=projv​u, and the perpendicular part is the remainder, u⊥=u−u∥\mathbf{u}_\perp=\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}_\parallelu⊥​=u−u∥​.

  4. Check that u⊥⋅v=0\mathbf{u}_\perp\cdot\mathbf{v}=0u⊥​⋅v=0 and u∥+u⊥=u\mathbf{u}_\parallel+\mathbf{u}_\perp=\mathbf{u}u∥​+u⊥​=u.

  5. The scalar projection, the signed length of the shadow, is u⋅v∥v∥=u⋅v^\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\left\|\mathbf{v}\right\|}=\mathbf{u}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{v}}∥v∥u⋅v​=u⋅v^.

  6. Work: a constant force F\mathbf{F}F moving through a displacement d\mathbf{d}d does work W=F⋅dW=\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{d}W=F⋅d. Its scalar component along the motion is F⋅d^=W/∥d∥\mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{d}}=W/\left\|\mathbf{d}\right\|F⋅d^=W/∥d∥.

Example A force F=(5,2,4)\mathbf{F}=(5,2,4)F=(5,2,4) (newtons) moves its point of application through d=(2,2,1)\mathbf{d}=(2,2,1)d=(2,2,1) (metres). Find the work done and the scalar component of F\mathbf{F}F along the motion, and resolve F\mathbf{F}F into parts along and across the motion.

W=F⋅d=10+4+4W=\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{d}=10+4+4W=F⋅d=10+4+4, so W=18 J\boxed{W=18\ \mathrm{J}}W=18 J​. With ∥d∥=4+4+1=3\left\|\mathbf{d}\right\|=\sqrt{4+4+1}=3∥d∥=4+4+1​=3, the scalar component along the motion is W/∥d∥=6 NW/\left\|\mathbf{d}\right\|=\boxed{6\ \mathrm{N}}W/∥d∥=6 N​.

For the parts, F⋅d=18\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{d}=18F⋅d=18 and ∥d∥2=9\left\|\mathbf{d}\right\|^2=9∥d∥2=9, so F∥=189(2,2,1)=(4,4,2)\mathbf{F}_\parallel=\tfrac{18}{9}(2,2,1)=(4,4,2)F∥​=918​(2,2,1)=(4,4,2), and the remainder is F⊥=(5,2,4)−(4,4,2)\mathbf{F}_\perp=(5,2,4)-(4,4,2)F⊥​=(5,2,4)−(4,4,2): F∥=(4,4,2) N,F⊥=(1,−2,2) N\boxed{\mathbf{F}_\parallel=(4,4,2)\ \mathrm{N}},\qquad\allowbreak \boxed{\mathbf{F}_\perp=(1,-2,2)\ \mathrm{N}}F∥​=(4,4,2) N​,F⊥​=(1,−2,2) N​

Check. F⊥⋅d=2−4+2=0\mathbf{F}_\perp\cdot\mathbf{d}=2-4+2=0F⊥​⋅d=2−4+2=0 and F∥+F⊥=(5,2,4)=F\mathbf{F}_\parallel+\mathbf{F}_\perp=(5,2,4)=\mathbf{F}F∥​+F⊥​=(5,2,4)=F. The parallel part has length ∥(4,4,2)∥=6\left\|(4,4,2)\right\|=6∥(4,4,2)∥=6, the scalar component, and Pythagoras holds: ∥F∥2=45=36+9\left\|\mathbf{F}\right\|^2=45=36+9∥F∥2=45=36+9.

Pitfalls

  • Dividing by ∥d∥\left\|\mathbf{d}\right\|∥d∥ instead of ∥d∥2\left\|\mathbf{d}\right\|^2∥d∥2. It gives 6(2,2,1)=(12,12,6)6(2,2,1)=(12,12,6)6(2,2,1)=(12,12,6), three times too long. The vector projection divides by the length squared, the scalar projection by the length.

  • Projecting the wrong way round. proj⁡dF\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{d}}\mathbf{F}projd​F lies along d\mathbf{d}d; proj⁡Fd\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{F}}\mathbf{d}projF​d lies along F\mathbf{F}F, and is a different vector.

  • Mixing up the two components. The scalar component is the number 666 N, the parallel part the vector (4,4,2)(4,4,2)(4,4,2) N; and work is a scalar, in joules.

4.3 The cross product: normal, area, volume, torque

Problem. In R3\mathbb{R}^3R3, find a vector perpendicular to two given vectors, the area of a parallelogram or a triangle, the volume of a parallelepiped, or a torque.

Method

  1. Compute u×v\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}u×v from its components u2v3−u3v2u_2v_3-u_3v_2u2​v3​−u3​v2​, u3v1−u1v3u_3v_1-u_1v_3u3​v1​−u1​v3​ and u1v2−u2v1u_1v_2-u_2v_1u1​v2​−u2​v1​, showing every product. The determinant with i,j,k\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}i,j,k in the top row is a way to remember them.

  2. Check: the result dotted with u\mathbf{u}u, and with v\mathbf{v}v, gives 000.

  3. Normal: u×v\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}u×v is perpendicular to both factors. Divide out any common factor; for a unit normal, divide by its length.

  4. Area: ∥u×v∥\left\|\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\right\|∥u×v∥ for the parallelogram on u\mathbf{u}u and v\mathbf{v}v, and half of it for the triangle. For a triangle ABCABCABC, take u=AB→\mathbf{u}=\overrightarrow{AB}u=AB and v=AC→\mathbf{v}=\overrightarrow{AC}v=AC.

  5. Volume: compute v×w\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{w}v×w first, then u⋅(v×w)\mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{w})u⋅(v×w). The volume of the parallelepiped is its absolute value, and 000 means the three vectors are coplanar.

  6. Torque: τ=r×F\bm{\tau}=\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}τ=r×F, by step 1, with r\mathbf{r}r the position of the point where F\mathbf{F}F acts, measured from the pivot.

Example Let A(0,1,1)A(0,1,1)A(0,1,1), B(2,4,−1)B(2,4,-1)B(2,4,−1), C(1,3,−1)C(1,3,-1)C(1,3,−1) and D(1,2,4)D(1,2,4)D(1,2,4). (a) Find a unit vector perpendicular to the plane of AAA, BBB and CCC, and the area of the triangle ABCABCABC. (b) Find the volume of the parallelepiped on AB→\overrightarrow{AB}AB, AC→\overrightarrow{AC}AC and AD→\overrightarrow{AD}AD. (c) Find the torque about a pivot of the force F=(3,0,−1)\mathbf{F}=(3,0,-1)F=(3,0,−1) (newtons) acting at r=(0,2,1)\mathbf{r}=(0,2,1)r=(0,2,1) (metres) from it.

(a) AB→=(2,3,−2)\overrightarrow{AB}=(2,3,-2)AB=(2,3,−2) and AC→=(1,2,−2)\overrightarrow{AC}=(1,2,-2)AC=(1,2,−2). The components of their cross product are 3⋅(−2)−(−2)⋅2=−23\cdot(-2)-(-2)\cdot2=-23⋅(−2)−(−2)⋅2=−2, (−2)⋅1−2⋅(−2)=2(-2)\cdot1-2\cdot(-2)=2(−2)⋅1−2⋅(−2)=2 and 2⋅2−3⋅1=12\cdot2-3\cdot1=12⋅2−3⋅1=1: AB→×AC→=(−2,2,1)\boxed{\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=(-2,2,1)}AB×AC=(−2,2,1)​ Check: AB→⋅(−2,2,1)=−4+6−2=0\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(-2,2,1)=-4+6-2=0AB⋅(−2,2,1)=−4+6−2=0 and AC→⋅(−2,2,1)=−2+4−2=0\overrightarrow{AC}\cdot(-2,2,1)=-2+4-2=0AC⋅(−2,2,1)=−2+4−2=0. Its length is 4+4+1=3\sqrt{4+4+1}=34+4+1​=3, so n^=±13(−2,2,1),area=32\boxed{\hat{\mathbf{n}}=\pm\tfrac13(-2,2,1)},\qquad\allowbreak \boxed{\text{area}=\tfrac32}n^=±31​(−2,2,1)​,area=23​​

(c) τ=r×F\bm{\tau}=\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}τ=r×F has components 2⋅(−1)−1⋅0=−22\cdot(-1)-1\cdot0=-22⋅(−1)−1⋅0=−2, 1⋅3−0⋅(−1)=31\cdot3-0\cdot(-1)=31⋅3−0⋅(−1)=3 and 0⋅0−2⋅3=−60\cdot0-2\cdot3=-60⋅0−2⋅3=−6: τ=(−2,3,−6) N m\boxed{\bm{\tau}=(-2,3,-6)\ \mathrm{N\,m}}τ=(−2,3,−6) Nm​ of magnitude 777 N m. 4.4 A line through two points; is a point on it?

Problem. Find the line through two points in vector, parametric or symmetric form, and decide whether a given point lies on it.

Method

  1. The direction is d=AB→\mathbf{d}=\overrightarrow{AB}d=AB: subtract the coordinates of AAA from those of BBB. A tidier multiple serves as well. The length ∥AB→∥\left\|\overrightarrow{AB}\right\|​AB​ is the distance from AAA to BBB.

  2. Take AAA as the base point, with position vector r0\mathbf{r}_0r0​. The vector form is r=r0+t d\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}_0+t\,\mathbf{d}r=r0​+td, and in coordinates the parametric form is x=x0+t d1x=x_0+t\,d_1x=x0​+td1​, y=y0+t d2y=y_0+t\,d_2y=y0​+td2​, z=z0+t d3z=z_0+t\,d_3z=z0​+td3​.

  3. If asked, eliminate ttt for the symmetric form x−x0d1=y−y0d2=z−z0d3\dfrac{x-x_0}{d_1}=\dfrac{y-y_0}{d_2}=\dfrac{z-z_0}{d_3}d1​x−x0​​=d2​y−y0​​=d3​z−z0​​, possible when no did_idi​ is 000.

  4. Check: some value of ttt returns BBB.

  5. Point test: solve for ttt from one coordinate, then put that ttt into the others. The point is on the line only if every coordinate matches.

AB→=(−4,2,6)=2(−2,1,3)\overrightarrow{AB}=(-4,2,6)=2(-2,1,3)AB=(−4,2,6)=2(−2,1,3), so AB=16+4+36=56=214AB=\sqrt{16+4+36}=\sqrt{56}=\boxed{2\sqrt{14}}AB=16+4+36​=56​=214​​, and the tidier direction is d=(−2,1,3)\mathbf{d}=(-2,1,3)d=(−2,1,3). With base point AAA, r=(3,1,−2)+t(−2,1,3)\boxed{\mathbf{r}=(3,1,-2)+t(-2,1,3)}r=(3,1,−2)+t(−2,1,3)​ that is, x=3−2tx=3-2tx=3−2t, y=1+ty=1+ty=1+t, z=−2+3tz=-2+3tz=−2+3t. Eliminating ttt, x−3−2=y−1=z+23\boxed{\frac{x-3}{-2}=y-1=\frac{z+2}{3}}−2x−3​=y−1=3z+2​​ Putting t=2t=2t=2 gives (3−4, 1+2, −2+6)=(−1,3,4)=B(3-4,\,1+2,\,-2+6)=(-1,3,4)=B(3−4,1+2,−2+6)=(−1,3,4)=B.

For DDD: 3−2t=13-2t=13−2t=1 gives t=1t=1t=1; then y=2y=2y=2 matches, but z=−2+3=1≠2z=-2+3=1\ne2z=−2+3=1=2, so D is not on the line\boxed{D\text{ is not on the line}}D is not on the line​.

4.5 A plane through three points

Problem. Find the plane through three points, in point-normal, Cartesian or parametric form.

Method

  1. Two vectors in the plane. With PPP as the base point, form PQ→\overrightarrow{PQ}PQ​ and PR→\overrightarrow{PR}PR.

  2. A normal, by the cross product: n=PQ→×PR→\mathbf{n}=\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}n=PQ​×PR (Method 4.3). Any nonzero multiple serves, so divide out a common factor.

  3. The equation. Write the point-normal form n⋅(r−r0)=0\mathbf{n}\cdot(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0)=0n⋅(r−r0​)=0 at PPP, that is a(x−x0)+b(y−y0)+c(z−z0)=0a(x-x_0)+b(y-y_0)+c(z-z_0)=0a(x−x0​)+b(y−y0​)+c(z−z0​)=0, and multiply it out to ax+by+cz=dax+by+cz=dax+by+cz=d, with d=n⋅r0d=\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{r}_0d=n⋅r0​.

  4. Check: all three points satisfy it.

  5. Parametric form, if asked: r=r0+s PQ→+t PR→\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}_0+s\,\overrightarrow{PQ}+t\,\overrightarrow{PR}r=r0​+sPQ​+tPR, with s,t∈Rs,t\in\mathbb{R}s,t∈R.

Why it works. A point r\mathbf{r}r lies in the plane exactly when r−r0\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0r−r0​ lies flat in it, that is, when it is orthogonal to n\mathbf{n}n. If PQ→×PR→=0\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}=\mathbf{0}PQ​×PR=0, the three points are on one line and do not fix a plane.

4.6 Where a line meets a plane; distance from a point to a plane

Problem. Find where a line meets a plane, or show that it misses the plane or lies in it; find the foot of the perpendicular from a point to a plane, and the distance.

Method

  1. Write the coordinates of a point of the line in terms of ttt: x=x0+t d1x=x_0+t\,d_1x=x0​+td1​, y=y0+t d2y=y_0+t\,d_2y=y0​+td2​, z=z0+t d3z=z_0+t\,d_3z=z0​+td3​.

  2. Substitute them into the plane’s equation, and solve for ttt.

  3. Put that ttt back into the line: it gives the crossing point. Check that the point satisfies the plane’s equation.

  4. If ttt cancels, then d⋅n=0\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{n}=0d⋅n=0 and the direction lies flat. The base point decides: on the plane, the line lies in it (every ttt works); off it, the line is parallel (no ttt works).

  5. Distance from a point p\mathbf{p}p: step from p\mathbf{p}p along the normal, p+t n\mathbf{p}+t\,\mathbf{n}p+tn. Substitute into the plane’s equation and solve for ttt; that point is the foot of the perpendicular.

  6. The distance is ∣t∣ ∥n∥\left|t\right|\,\left\|\mathbf{n}\right\|∣t∣∥n∥. Check it by the formula ∣ap1+bp2+cp3−d∣∥n∥\dfrac{\left|ap_1+bp_2+cp_3-d\right|}{\left\|\mathbf{n}\right\|}∥n∥∣ap1​+bp2​+cp3​−d∣​.

Example Take the plane 2x−3y+6z=52x-3y+6z=52x−3y+6z=5. (a) Where does the line r=(3,1,0)+t(1,1,0)\mathbf{r}=(3,1,0)+t(1,1,0)r=(3,1,0)+t(1,1,0) meet it? (b) And the line r=(1,1,1)+t(3,0,−1)\mathbf{r}=(1,1,1)+t(3,0,-1)r=(1,1,1)+t(3,0,−1)? (c) Find the foot of the perpendicular from P(2,−1,2)P(2,-1,2)P(2,−1,2) to the plane, and the distance from PPP to it.

(a) A point of the line is (3+t, 1+t, 0)(3+t,\,1+t,\,0)(3+t,1+t,0). Substituting, 2(3+t)−3(1+t)+6⋅0=5  ⟺  3−t=5,2(3+t)-3(1+t)+6\cdot0=5 \;\Longleftrightarrow\;3-t=5 ,2(3+t)−3(1+t)+6⋅0=5⟺3−t=5, so t=−2t=-2t=−2, and the crossing point is (1,−1,0)\boxed{(1,-1,0)}(1,−1,0)​. It satisfies 2+3+0=52+3+0=52+3+0=5.

(b) A point of the line is (1+3t, 1, 1−t)(1+3t,\,1,\,1-t)(1+3t,1,1−t). Substituting, 2(1+3t)−3+6(1−t)=5  ⟺  5=5,2(1+3t)-3+6(1-t)=5 \;\Longleftrightarrow\;5=5 ,2(1+3t)−3+6(1−t)=5⟺5=5, which holds for every ttt. The ttt cancelled because d⋅n=6+0−6=0\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{n}=6+0-6=0d⋅n=6+0−6=0, and the base point is on the plane (2−3+6=52-3+6=52−3+6=5), so the line lies in the plane\boxed{\text{the line lies in the plane}}the line lies in the plane​.

(c) The normal is n=(2,−3,6)\mathbf{n}=(2,-3,6)n=(2,−3,6), with ∥n∥=4+9+36=7\left\|\mathbf{n}\right\|=\sqrt{4+9+36}=7∥n∥=4+9+36​=7. Step from PPP: p+t n=(2+2t, −1−3t, 2+6t)\mathbf{p}+t\,\mathbf{n}=(2+2t,\,-1-3t,\,2+6t)p+tn=(2+2t,−1−3t,2+6t) lies on the plane when 2(2+2t)−3(−1−3t)+6(2+6t)=5,2(2+2t)-3(-1-3t)+6(2+6t)=5 ,2(2+2t)−3(−1−3t)+6(2+6t)=5, that is 19+49t=519+49t=519+49t=5, so t=−1449=−27t=-\tfrac{14}{49}=-\tfrac27t=−4914​=−72​. The foot is (2,−1,2)−27(2,−3,6)(2,-1,2)-\tfrac27(2,-3,6)(2,−1,2)−72​(2,−3,6): F=(107,−17,27)\boxed{F=\bigl(\tfrac{10}{7},-\tfrac17,\tfrac27\bigr)}F=(710​,−71​,72​)​ and the distance is ∣t∣ ∥n∥=27⋅7=2\left|t\right|\,\left\|\mathbf{n}\right\|=\tfrac27\cdot7=\boxed{2}∣t∣∥n∥=72​⋅7=2​.

Check. The formula gives ∣2⋅2−3⋅(−1)+6⋅2−5∣7=147=2\dfrac{\left|2\cdot 2-3\cdot(-1)+6\cdot 2-5\right|}{7}=\dfrac{14}{7}=27∣2⋅2−3⋅(−1)+6⋅2−5∣​=714​=2, and the foot is on the plane: 207+37+127=5\tfrac{20}{7}+\tfrac37+\tfrac{12}{7}=5720​+73​+712​=5.

Pitfalls

  • Stopping at ttt. In (a), t=−2t=-2t=−2 is a parameter value, not the point: put it back into the line.

  • Calling the line in (b) parallel because d⋅n=0\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{n}=0d⋅n=0. That says only that the direction lies flat; the base point decides between parallel and contained.

  • Giving ∣t∣=27\left|t\right|=\tfrac27∣t∣=72​ as the distance. The step was t nt\,\mathbf{n}tn, so the distance is ∣t∣ ∥n∥=2\left|t\right|\,\left\|\mathbf{n}\right\|=2∣t∣∥n∥=2, unless n\mathbf{n}n is a unit vector.

Unit 5 · Matrices

The notes · The problems

Five methods, and each starts from the sizes and the shape of the matrix. A short proof about matrices (a trace identity, a property of the inverse) is a single move: state the goal, rewrite it with the named rules (associativity, the transpose rules, uniqueness of the inverse) and end with a concluding sentence.

Which method?

The question asks for Method
whether a sum or a product is defined, and its size 5.1, compare the sizes first
a product, a transpose or a trace 5.1, row times column
a 3×33\times33×3 determinant with zeros in it 5.2, expand along the row or column with most zeros
the value of a parameter that makes a matrix singular 5.2, solve det⁡=0\det=0det=0
the inverse of a 2×22\times22×2 matrix 5.3, swap, negate, divide by det⁡\detdet
the inverse of a 3×33\times33×3 matrix 5.3, cofactors and the adjugate
the inverse of a triangular or larger matrix 5.3, row-reduce ( A∣I )(\,\mathbf{A}\mid\mathbf{I}\,)(A∣I)
the solution of a system, A−1\mathbf{A}^{-1}A−1 known 5.4, variant: x=A−1b\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}x=A−1b
the solution of a system, otherwise 5.4, Gaussian elimination
whether a system has one, no or infinitely many solutions 5.4, read the echelon form, 0=c0=c0=c first
the matrix of a map of the plane, or of two maps in turn 5.5, columns are the images of i,j\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}i,j
the effect of a map on area and orientation 5.5, the sign and size of det⁡\detdet

5.1 Products, transpose and trace: check the sizes first

Problem. Decide whether a sum or a product of matrices is defined, and compute it; find a transpose or a trace.

Method

  1. Write down the size of every matrix, m×nm\times nm×n (mmm rows, nnn columns).

  2. Sum, difference or scalar multiple: the sizes must be equal. Then work entry by entry.

  3. Product AB\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}AB: write the sizes as (m×n)(n′×p)(m\times n)(n'\times p)(m×n)(n′×p). If n≠n′n\ne n'n=n′ the product is undefined: stop. Otherwise it is m×pm\times pm×p.

  4. The (i,j)(i,j)(i,j) entry of AB\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}AB is row iii of A\mathbf{A}A dotted with column jjj of B\mathbf{B}B.

  5. Transpose: swap rows and columns, so the (i,j)(i,j)(i,j) entry of AT\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{T}}AT is ajia_{ji}aji​. For a product, (AB)T=BTAT(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{T}}(AB)T=BTAT.

  6. Trace, of a square matrix only: the sum of the diagonal entries.

Example Let A=(2−1013−2)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0\\1&3&-2\end{pmatrix}A=(21​−13​0−2​) and B=(140−132)\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\0&-1\\3&2\end{pmatrix}B=​103​4−12​​. Which of A+B\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}A+B, A+BT\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}A+BT, AB\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}AB and BA\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}BA are defined? Compute A+BT\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}A+BT, AB\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}AB and tr(AB)\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})tr(AB).

A\mathbf{A}A is 2×32\times32×3 and B\mathbf{B}B is 3×23\times23×2, so A+B is undefined\boxed{\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}\ \text{is undefined}}A+B is undefined​. BT\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}BT is 2×32\times32×3, so A+BT\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}A+BT is defined and 2×32\times32×3. The product (2×3)(3×2)(2\times3)(3\times2)(2×3)(3×2) has matching inner sizes and is 2×22\times22×2; BA\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}BA is (3×2)(2×3)(3\times2)(2\times3)(3×2)(2×3), so it is 3×33\times33×3. Entrywise, A+BT=(2−1013−2)+(1034−12)=(3−13520).\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}} =\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0\\1&3&-2\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}1&0&3\\4&-1&2\end{pmatrix} =\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}3&-1&3\\5&2&0\end{pmatrix}}.A+BT=(21​−13​0−2​)+(14​0−1​32​)=(35​−12​30​)​. Row times column, AB=(2+0+08+1+01+0−64−3−4)=(29−5−3),\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix}2+0+0&8+1+0\\1+0-6&4-3-4\end{pmatrix} =\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}2&9\\-5&-3\end{pmatrix}},AB=(2+0+01+0−6​8+1+04−3−4​)=(2−5​9−3​)​, and the trace is the diagonal sum, 2+(−3)2+(-3)2+(−3): tr(AB)=−1\boxed{\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})=-1}tr(AB)=−1​.

Check. The cyclic property says tr(BA)=tr(AB)\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A})=\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})tr(BA)=tr(AB), although BA\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}BA is 3×33\times33×3. Its diagonal entries are 1⋅2+4⋅1=61\cdot2+4\cdot1=61⋅2+4⋅1=6, 0⋅(−1)+(−1)⋅3=−30\cdot(-1)+(-1)\cdot3=-30⋅(−1)+(−1)⋅3=−3 and 3⋅0+2⋅(−2)=−43\cdot0+2\cdot(-2)=-43⋅0+2⋅(−2)=−4, and 6−3−4=−16-3-4=-16−3−4=−1.

Pitfalls

  • Adding A\mathbf{A}A and B\mathbf{B}B because both have six entries. The sizes 2×32\times32×3 and 3×23\times23×2 differ, so the sum does not exist.

  • Multiplying entry by entry, or giving a product the inner sizes: the size of BA\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}BA comes from the outer ones, 3×33\times33×3.

  • Transposing a product without reversing it. Here ATBT\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}ATBT is 3×33\times33×3, so it cannot be (AB)T(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^{\mathsf{T}}(AB)T, which is 2×22\times22×2.

5.2 Determinants by cofactor expansion; the parameter that makes a matrix singular

Problem. Evaluate the determinant of a 2×22\times22×2 or 3×33\times33×3 matrix; decide whether the matrix is invertible; find the values of a parameter for which it is singular.

Method

  1. For a 2×22\times22×2 matrix, det⁡(abcd)=ad−bc\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}=ad-bcdet(ac​bd​)=ad−bc.

  2. For a 3×33\times33×3 matrix, choose the row or column with the most zeros (the first row if none stands out).

  3. Write each entry of that row or column times its cofactor Cij=(−1)i+jMijC_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}Cij​=(−1)i+jMij​. The sign follows the checkerboard +−+−+−+−+\begin{smallmatrix}+&-&+\\-&+&-\\+&-&+\end{smallmatrix}+−+​−+−​+−+​, and the minor MijM_{ij}Mij​ is the 2×22\times22×2 determinant left when row iii and column jjj are deleted. A zero entry drops out.

  4. Evaluate the 2×22\times22×2 minors and add up.

  5. The matrix is invertible exactly when det⁡≠0\det\ne0det=0; det⁡=0\det=0det=0 means singular.

  6. For a parameter kkk: find det⁡\detdet as an expression in kkk, set it equal to 000 and solve. Those values, and only those, make the matrix singular.

Variants. A triangular matrix has determinant equal to the product of its diagonal entries, with no expansion needed.

Example (a) Evaluate det⁡A\det\mathbf{A}detA for A=(21−3405−102)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&-3\\4&0&5\\-1&0&2\end{pmatrix}A=​24−1​100​−352​​. (b) For which kkk is B=(k103k2011)\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix}k&1&0\\3&k&2\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}B=​k30​1k1​021​​ singular?

(a) Column 2 has two zeros, so expand along it. Only the entry a12=1a_{12}=1a12​=1 survives, and position (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) carries the sign −-−: det⁡A=−1∣45−12∣=−(8+5)=−13.\det\mathbf{A}=-1\begin{vmatrix}4&5\\-1&2\end{vmatrix}=-(8+5) =\boxed{-13}.detA=−1​4−1​52​​=−(8+5)=−13​. (b) Expand along the first row, whose third entry is 000: det⁡B=k∣k211∣−1∣3201∣=k(k−2)−3.\det\mathbf{B}=k\begin{vmatrix}k&2\\1&1\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}3&2\\0&1\end{vmatrix} =k(k-2)-3 .detB=k​k1​21​​−1​30​21​​=k(k−2)−3. So det⁡B=k2−2k−3=(k−3)(k+1)\det\mathbf{B}=k^2-2k-3=(k-3)(k+1)detB=k2−2k−3=(k−3)(k+1), which is 000 for k=−1 or k=3\boxed{k=-1\text{ or }k=3}k=−1 or k=3​.

Check. (a) Expanding along the first row instead gives 2⋅0−1⋅13+(−3)⋅0=−132\cdot0-1\cdot13+(-3)\cdot0=-132⋅0−1⋅13+(−3)⋅0=−13. (b) At k=3k=3k=3 the rows of B\mathbf{B}B are (3,1,0)(3,1,0)(3,1,0), (3,3,2)(3,3,2)(3,3,2), (0,1,1)(0,1,1)(0,1,1). The second is the first plus twice the third, so the three rows lie in one plane and the determinant must be 000.

Pitfalls

  • Dropping the checkerboard sign. In (a) the cofactor of a12a_{12}a12​ is −13-13−13, so det⁡A=−13\det\mathbf{A}=-13detA=−13, not 131313.

  • Using the diagonal product on a matrix that is not triangular.

  • Losing a root: k2−2k−3=0k^2-2k-3=0k2−2k−3=0 has two solutions, and both make B\mathbf{B}B singular.

5.3 The inverse: the 2×22\times22×2 formula, cofactors, or row reduction

Problem. Find the inverse of a square matrix, or show that it has none.

Method

  1. Find det⁡A\det\mathbf{A}detA (Method 5.2). If it is 000 there is no inverse: stop.

  2. A 2×22\times22×2 matrix: swap the diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal ones, and divide by the determinant, (abcd)−1=1ad−bc(d−b−ca)\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}^{-1}=\dfrac1{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}(ac​bd​)−1=ad−bc1​(d−c​−ba​).

  3. A 3×33\times33×3 matrix by cofactors: find all nine cofactors Cij=(−1)i+jMijC_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}Cij​=(−1)i+jMij​ and write the cofactor matrix C=(Cij)\mathbf{C}=(C_{ij})C=(Cij​).

  4. Transpose it to get the adjugate, adj⁡(A)=CT\operatorname{adj}(\mathbf{A})=\mathbf{C}^{\mathsf{T}}adj(A)=CT, and divide by the determinant: A−1=1det⁡Aadj⁡(A)\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{\det\mathbf{A}}\operatorname{adj}(\mathbf{A})A−1=detA1​adj(A).

  5. Or by row reduction: write ( A∣I )(\,\mathbf{A}\mid\mathbf{I}\,)(A∣I) and apply row operations until the left block is I\mathbf{I}I (echelon form, then scale each pivot to 111 and clear above it). The right block is then A−1\mathbf{A}^{-1}A−1.

  6. Check one product: AA−1=I\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\mathbf{I}AA−1=I.

Example Invert (a) P=(3−24−1)\mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix}3&-2\\4&-1\end{pmatrix}P=(34​−2−1​) and (b) A=(10033−121−1)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\3&3&-1\\2&1&-1\end{pmatrix}A=​132​031​0−1−1​​.

(a) det⁡P=3(−1)−(−2)(4)=5≠0\det\mathbf{P}=3(-1)-(-2)(4)=5\ne0detP=3(−1)−(−2)(4)=5=0. Swap, negate and divide by 555: P−1=15(−12−43)\boxed{\mathbf{P}^{-1}=\frac15\begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\-4&3\end{pmatrix}}P−1=51​(−1−4​23​)​ (b) Expand along the first row: det⁡A=1⋅∣3−11−1∣=−2\det\mathbf{A}=1\cdot\begin{vmatrix}3&-1\\1&-1\end{vmatrix}=-2detA=1⋅​31​−1−1​​=−2. 5.4 Gaussian elimination and reading the echelon form

Problem. Solve a linear system Ax=b\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}Ax=b, or decide whether it has one solution, none or infinitely many.

Method

  1. Write the augmented matrix ( A∣b )(\,\mathbf{A}\mid\mathbf{b}\,)(A∣b).

  2. Reduce it to echelon form with labelled row operations Ri→Ri+kRjR_i\to R_i+kR_jRi​→Ri​+kRj​, stacked when done at once. Keep the entries integers (a step such as R2→2R2+3R1R_2\to2R_2+3R_1R2​→2R2​+3R1​ is allowed), and swap two rows if a pivot is 000.

  3. Look first for a row ( 0 ⋯ 0∣c )(\,0\ \cdots\ 0\mid c\,)(0 ⋯ 0∣c) with c≠0c\ne0c=0. It reads 0=c0=c0=c: there is no solution. Stop.

  4. Otherwise count the leading entries. With one for each unknown the solution is unique: back-substitute, from the last row up.

  5. With fewer leading entries than unknowns, set the free unknown equal to ttt, back-substitute, and write the solution as x=p+t d\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{p}+t\,\mathbf{d}x=p+td, t∈Rt\in\mathbb{R}t∈R: a line.

  6. Check the answer in every original equation (for a line, at t=0t=0t=0 and t=1t=1t=1).

Variants. Gauss–Jordan continues from the echelon form: scale each pivot to 111 and clear above it, to reach ( I∣x )(\,\mathbf{I}\mid\mathbf{x}\,)(I∣x) and read the solution off. The inverse method solves x=A−1b\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}x=A−1b when A−1\mathbf{A}^{-1}A−1 is known. With P−1\mathbf{P}^{-1}P−1 from Method 5.3, the system 3x−2y=43x-2y=43x−2y=4, 4x−y=74x-y=74x−y=7 gives (xy)=15(−12−43)(47)=15(−4+14−16+21)=(21).\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\frac15\begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\-4&3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}4\\7\end{pmatrix} =\frac15\begin{pmatrix}-4+14\\-16+21\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix} .(xy​)=51​(−1−4​23​)(47​)=51​(−4+14−16+21​)=(21​). For a square system, det⁡A≠0\det\mathbf{A}\ne0detA=0 guarantees exactly one solution; det⁡=0\det=0det=0 leaves none or infinitely many, and only the echelon form says which.

Example For which values of aaa and bbb does the system x+2y−z=2,2x+5y+3z=7,3x+7y+az=bx+2y-z=2,\qquad\allowbreak 2x+5y+3z=7,\qquad\allowbreak 3x+7y+az=bx+2y−z=2,2x+5y+3z=7,3x+7y+az=b have exactly one solution, none, or infinitely many? Solve it in the last case.

5.5 A matrix as a transformation of the plane

Problem. Find the matrix of a map of the plane, or of two maps done in turn; find the image of a point or a shape; describe the effect on area and orientation.

Method

  1. The columns of the matrix are the images of i=(1,0)\mathbf{i}=(1,0)i=(1,0) and j=(0,1)\mathbf{j}=(0,1)j=(0,1). Or take it from the standard list: rotation by θ\thetaθ, (cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ)\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}(cosθsinθ​−sinθcosθ​); reflection in y=xy=xy=x; enlargement; stretch; shear.

  2. “Do S\mathbf{S}S, then R\mathbf{R}R” is the single matrix RS\mathbf{R}\mathbf{S}RS: the map done first stands on the right.

  3. Apply the matrix to the vector, or to each corner of a shape. The edges between corners go to the edges between their images.

  4. Read the determinant: ∣det⁡∣\left|\det\right|∣det∣ is the factor by which areas scale, a negative det⁡\detdet flips the orientation, and det⁡=0\det=0det=0 collapses the plane onto a line (the map is not invertible).

  5. To name a map, see where it sends i\mathbf{i}i and j\mathbf{j}j.

Example Let S=(1201)\mathbf{S}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}S=(10​21​), the shear (x,y)↦(x+2y,y)(x,y)\mapsto(x+2y,y)(x,y)↦(x+2y,y), and let T\mathbf{T}T be the map that sends i\mathbf{i}i to (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) and j\mathbf{j}j to (2,−1)(2,-1)(2,−1). (a) Find T\mathbf{T}T. (b) Find the matrix M\mathbf{M}M of “first S\mathbf{S}S, then T\mathbf{T}T”. (c) Find the image of the triangle with corners (0,0)(0,0)(0,0), (3,0)(3,0)(3,0), (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) under M\mathbf{M}M, and the effect on area and orientation.

(a) The images of i\mathbf{i}i and j\mathbf{j}j are the columns: T=(121−1)\boxed{\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}}T=(11​2−1​)​.

(b) The shear is done first, so it stands on the right: M=TS=(121−1)(1201)=(1411)\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{T}\mathbf{S}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix} =\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\1&1\end{pmatrix}}M=TS=(11​2−1​)(10​21​)=(11​41​)​ (c) M\mathbf{M}M fixes (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) and sends (3,0)(3,0)(3,0) to (3,3)(3,3)(3,3) and (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) to (1+8, 1+2)(1+8,\,1+2)(1+8,1+2). The image is the triangle with corners (0,0), (3,3), (9,3)\boxed{(0,0),\ (3,3),\ (9,3)}(0,0), (3,3), (9,3)​. Since det⁡M=1−4=−3\boxed{\det\mathbf{M}=1-4=-3}detM=1−4=−3​, areas are multiplied by 333 and the orientation is flipped.

Check. Half the 2×22\times22×2 determinant of the two edges from (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) gives the area. Before: 12(3⋅2−0⋅1)=3\tfrac12(3\cdot2-0\cdot1)=321​(3⋅2−0⋅1)=3. After: 12(3⋅3−3⋅9)=−9\tfrac12(3\cdot3-3\cdot9)=-921​(3⋅3−3⋅9)=−9: the area is 9=3×39=3\times39=3×3, and the sign has reversed.

Pitfalls

  • Multiplying in the order of the words. ST=(301−1)\mathbf{S}\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}ST=(31​0−1​) applies T\mathbf{T}T first, and sends (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) to (3,−1)(3,-1)(3,−1), not (9,3)(9,3)(9,3).

  • Writing the images of i\mathbf{i}i and j\mathbf{j}j as the rows instead of the columns.

  • Reading det⁡M=−3\det\mathbf{M}=-3detM=−3 as a negative area. The area scales by ∣det⁡∣=3\left|\det\right|=3∣det∣=3; the sign is the orientation.

Unit 6 · Eigensystems

The notes · The problems

Six methods, and the first is a step in all the others. True-or-false questions and short proofs are not a method: answer each with a one-line reason that cites a result from the notes, or with one concrete counterexample, and set a proof out as set-up, derivation, conclusion.

6.1 The eigensystem: 2×22\times22×2, 3×33\times33×3, complex eigenvalues

Problem. Find the eigenvalues of a square matrix and an eigenvector for each, real or complex.

Method

  1. Write det⁡(A−λI)\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})det(A−λI) and expand it: a 2×22\times22×2 directly, a 3×33\times33×3 along the row or column with the most zeros.

  2. Factor the characteristic polynomial and name its roots λ1,λ2,…\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dotsλ1​,λ2​,…: these are the eigenvalues. A real 2×22\times22×2 with a negative discriminant gives a complex pair a±b ia\pm b\,\mathrm{i}a±bi.

  3. For each eigenvalue in turn, write (A−λI)v=0(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}(A−λI)v=0. For a 2×22\times22×2, one row is enough: read off how v1v_1v1​ and v2v_2v2​ are related and choose a simple v\mathbf{v}v.

  4. For a 3×33\times33×3, row-reduce A−λI\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I}A−λI, or read the equations off directly when the zeros make them immediate. Set the free unknown to 111 and back-substitute.

  5. For a complex pair, find the eigenvector of a+b ia+b\,\mathrm{i}a+bi from row 1; the eigenvector of a−b ia-b\,\mathrm{i}a−bi is its conjugate. Only if asked: ∣λ∣\left|\lambda\right|∣λ∣ sets the growth per step and arg⁡λ\arg\lambdaargλ the angle turned.

  6. Check one pair with Av=λv\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}Av=λv, and the eigenvalues with ∑λi=trA\sum\lambda_i=\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf{A}∑λi​=trA and ∏λi=det⁡A\prod\lambda_i=\det\mathbf{A}∏λi​=detA.

Pitfalls

  • Subtracting λ\lambdaλ from one diagonal entry only, or from every entry. It comes off each diagonal entry and nowhere else.

  • Row-reducing A−λI\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I}A−λI to a matrix with no zero row. Then the only solution is 0\mathbf{0}0, and λ\lambdaλ is not an eigenvalue: recheck the characteristic polynomial.

6.2 Is it diagonalisable? Multiplicities

Problem. Decide whether a matrix is diagonalisable, giving the algebraic and geometric multiplicity of each eigenvalue.

Method

  1. Find the eigenvalues (Method 6.1), and the algebraic multiplicity of each: how many times it repeats as a root. A triangular matrix has its diagonal entries as eigenvalues.

  2. If the nnn eigenvalues are distinct, the matrix is diagonalisable. Stop.

  3. For each repeated eigenvalue, solve (A−λI)v=0(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}(A−λI)v=0 and count the free unknowns: that is its geometric multiplicity, the number of independent eigenvectors.

  4. Compare. If geometric === algebraic for every eigenvalue, the matrix is diagonalisable. If any eigenvalue falls short, it is defective and cannot be diagonalised.

Why it works. An n×nn\times nn×n matrix is diagonalisable exactly when it has nnn independent eigenvectors. Eigenvectors of distinct eigenvalues are independent, and the geometric multiplicity never exceeds the algebraic one, so a simple root always gives exactly one eigenvector. Only a repeated root can fall short, and a real symmetric matrix never does.

Example Are these diagonalisable? A=(400121−123),B=(400121123).\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}4&0&0\\1&2&1\\-1&2&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\allowbreak \mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix}4&0&0\\1&2&1\\1&2&3\end{pmatrix}.A=​41−1​022​013​​,B=​411​022​013​​. Expand along row 1. The two matrices differ only in the (3,1)(3,1)(3,1) entry, which the expansion never uses, so both have det⁡(A−λI)=(4−λ)[(2−λ)(3−λ)−2]=(4−λ)(λ−1)(λ−4).\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=(4-\lambda)\bigl[(2-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-2\bigr] =(4-\lambda)(\lambda-1)(\lambda-4).det(A−λI)=(4−λ)[(2−λ)(3−λ)−2]=(4−λ)(λ−1)(λ−4). So λ=4\lambda=4λ=4 has algebraic multiplicity 222, and the simple root λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 gives one eigenvector. For λ=4\lambda=4λ=4, A−4I=(0001−21−12−1),B−4I=(0001−2112−1).\mathbf{A}-4\mathbf{I}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\1&-2&1\\-1&2&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\allowbreak \mathbf{B}-4\mathbf{I}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\1&-2&1\\1&2&-1\end{pmatrix}.A−4I=​01−1​0−22​01−1​​,B−4I=​011​0−22​01−1​​. 6.3 Diagonalising, and powers of a matrix

Problem. Write A=PDP−1\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{P}^{-1}A=PDP−1, and use it to find a closed form for Ak\mathbf{A}^kAk.

Method

  1. Find the eigenvalues and an eigenvector for each (Method 6.1).

  2. Put the eigenvectors in the columns of P\mathbf{P}P, and the eigenvalues on the diagonal of D\mathbf{D}D, in the same order.

  3. Compute det⁡P\det\mathbf{P}detP, and P−1\mathbf{P}^{-1}P−1 by the 2×22\times22×2 formula: swap the diagonal entries, negate the other two, divide by det⁡P\det\mathbf{P}detP.

  5. Multiply PDk\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^kPDk first, then multiply the result by P−1\mathbf{P}^{-1}P−1.

  6. Check that k=1k=1k=1 gives A\mathbf{A}A back.

6.5 Symmetric and Hermitian matrices: orthogonal diagonalisation, PCA

Problem. For a real symmetric matrix, find an orthogonal Q\mathbf{Q}Q with A=QDQT\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{Q}^{\mathsf{T}}A=QDQT, and read off the principal axes; for a Hermitian matrix, find its real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.

Method

  1. Check the structure: AT=A\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{A}AT=A for a real matrix; H†=H\mathbf{H}^{\dagger}=\mathbf{H}H†=H for a complex one (a real diagonal, and conjugates across it).

  2. Solve the characteristic equation. For a Hermitian matrix the off-diagonal product is zz‾=∣z∣2z\overline{z}=\left|z\right|^2zz=∣z∣2. The eigenvalues come out real.

  3. Find an eigenvector for each from row 1, choosing v2v_2v2​ to clear any fraction.

  4. Check that the eigenvectors are orthogonal: each pair has dot product 000. For complex vectors use u†v=u1‾v1+u2‾v2\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{v}=\overline{u_1}v_1+\overline{u_2}v_2u†v=u1​​v1​+u2​​v2​, not the plain product.

  5. Divide each eigenvector by its length. These are the columns of Q\mathbf{Q}Q, with the eigenvalues in D\mathbf{D}D in the same order. Then QTQ=I\mathbf{Q}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{I}QTQ=I and A=QDQT\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{Q}^{\mathsf{T}}A=QDQT.

  6. PCA: for a covariance matrix, the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue is the first principal axis, and it carries the share λ/trA\lambda/\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf{A}λ/trA of the total variance.

Example (a) Orthogonally diagonalise the covariance matrix A=(3226)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\2&6\end{pmatrix}A=(32​26​), and give its first principal axis and the share of the variance it carries. Row 1 reads v1+2v2=0v_1+2v_2=0v1​+2v2​=0 for λ1\lambda_1λ1​, giving (2,−1)T(2,-1)^{\mathsf{T}}(2,−1)T, and −4v1+2v2=0-4v_1+2v_2=0−4v1​+2v2​=0 for λ2\lambda_2λ2​, giving (1,2)T(1,2)^{\mathsf{T}}(1,2)T. The total variance is trA=9\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf{A}=9trA=9, so it carries 79≈77.8%\boxed{\tfrac79\approx77.8\%}97​≈77.8%​.

6.6 A Markov chain’s long run

Problem. Set up the transition matrix of a Markov chain; find its steady state, a closed form for xn\mathbf{x}_nxn​, and whether the chain settles.

Method

  1. Build P\mathbf{P}P: column jjj lists the probabilities of moving from state jjj. Check that each column sums to one.

  2. λ1=1\lambda_1=1λ1​=1 always. Find λ2\lambda_2λ2​ from the characteristic equation; for a 2×22\times22×2, λ1+λ2=trP\lambda_1+\lambda_2=\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbf{P}λ1​+λ2​=trP checks it.

  3. Steady state: solve (P−I)x=0(\mathbf{P}-\mathbf{I})\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}(P−I)x=0, scale x\mathbf{x}x so its entries sum to one, and check Px∞=x∞\mathbf{P}\mathbf{x}_\infty=\mathbf{x}_\inftyPx∞​=x∞​.

  4. Closed form: find the eigenvector v2\mathbf{v}_2v2​ of λ2\lambda_2λ2​, and write x0=c1x∞+c2v2\mathbf{x}_0=c_1\mathbf{x}_\infty+c_2\mathbf{v}_2x0​=c1​x∞​+c2​v2​. Since v2\mathbf{v}_2v2​ sums to zero, c1=1c_1=1c1​=1 for every probability start, and xn=x∞+c2λ2nv2\mathbf{x}_n=\mathbf{x}_\infty+c_2\lambda_2^n\mathbf{v}_2xn​=x∞​+c2​λ2n​v2​.

  5. Long run: the chain settles to x∞\mathbf{x}_\inftyx∞​ from every start when λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 is a simple root and every other eigenvalue has ∣λ∣<1\left|\lambda\right|<1∣λ∣<1. A second eigenvalue of modulus 111 (such as −1-1−1) can keep it moving for ever.

Example Each day a machine is either working or under repair. A working machine is still working the next day with probability 0.90.90.9; one under repair is working again the next day with probability 0.30.30.3. It starts under repair. Pitfalls

  • Putting the from-states in the rows. That builds PT\mathbf{P}^{\mathsf{T}}PT, whose columns here sum to 1.21.21.2 and 0.80.80.8: the column check catches it.

  • Giving the direction (3,1)(3,1)(3,1) as the steady state. A distribution sums to one: (0.75,0.25)(0.75,0.25)(0.75,0.25).

  • Promising convergence without checking the other eigenvalues. The swap (0110)\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}(01​10​) has eigenvalues ±1\pm1±1 and oscillates for ever, and I\mathbf{I}I has λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 twice and never forgets its start.
